catalog_quote: [Isukul n.d., p. 9, sec. 2.0] Agholo is a tone language. A tone language is a language that makes use of contrasts of pitch to signal a meaning difference between two or more words that are identical in shape with respect to their vowel and consonant combinations. The contrasting tones are: Level Tones: Low [ `] (unmarked in this work) High [ ´] (marked) Downstep [Õ] (marked between syllables) Gliding Tone: Falling tone [ ^] (marked) The low tone is the most common tone. For this reason, it is unmarked in this orthography I have proposed. Of the four tones, the falling tone has the most restricted distribution. It is found only word-finally. ... [sec. 2.1] Tone plays a role in lexical differentiation. Although the following words are spelt in the same way, they are pronounced with different tones. The difference in tone signals a difference in meaning. [ẹgi 'house fly' LL vs ẹgí 'journey' LH; ilu 'lie' LL vs ílu 'proverb' HL] ... The difference between a noun and a verb is sometimes indicated by tone only. ... [Lawson-Ikuru 2022: 173] Findings from the analysis reveal that both low (L) and high (H) tones are underlyingly present, the falling contour can be simplified to either a L or H tone with the potential of moving to final positions. Mid tone is quite inactive in underlying contrast and the rising tone is only discovered in constructions and not in words in isolation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogbia is described as a lexical tone language with two underlying level tones (Low, High), a derived falling contour, no underlying Mid, and a rising tone only in connected constructions; tone distinguishes lexical items and word classes (L-L nouns vs H-L verbs). No statement about word stress or accent placement is made in the accessible pages, and the family overview (Kari 2017: 'all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system', H/L plus downstep) likewise never mentions stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: falling contour 'can be simplified to either a L or H tone with the potential of moving to final positions'; rising tone absent in isolation forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/underlying tone on words in isolation and in grammatical constructions (noun classes, plurals, derivatives, compounds, verbal categories, reduplication), based on auditory analysis of three adult speakers; dialect of the speakers not stated in pp. 173-174. Only pp. 173-174 of 173-185 were accessible; a stress remark later in the chapter cannot be excluded but the chapter's topic is tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Lawson-Ikuru 2022 says only 'Ogbia (Niger-Congo)', three adult speakers, dialect unstated in the accessible pages. The Isukul works describe the Agholo (Kolo, Kolo Creek) dialect of Ogbia; Blench 2008/Kari 2017 list Ogbia dialects as Agholo (Kolo), Oloibiri, Anyama (Anyama unattested). All fall under glottocode ogbi1239 (ISO ogb); Glottolog has no separate dialect codes that I verified.

tone_statements.quote: Three tone levels make up the tonal system in Ogbia plus a downstep that rarely occurs (Isukul 2009:39). The tones are the high, low and mid. The mid tone is unmarked here. Data gathered in this work is from the Otakeme variety which is spoken by the Olobiri group in Ogbia.
tone_statements.summary: Noun-class article; adopts three level tones (high, low, mid; mid unmarked) plus a rare downstep from Isukul 2009 for its own Otakeme data; c. 250 tone-marked forms pp. 36-45; no TBU or stress.

sources.note: Nothing about stress in pp. 173-174. Treats Ogbia as a tone language: underlying L and H tones, falling contour reducible to L or H, mid tone inactive underlyingly, rising tone only in constructions; minimal pairs L-L nouns vs H-L verbs (p.174). Remaining pp. 175-185 paywalled, not seen.

sources.note: No mention of stress or accent anywhere. Sec. 3.4 Tone (p.11): quotes Alex (1989:24) 'all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system' (H, L, plus downstep); tone examples given only for Abuan, Odual, Ogbronuagum, not Ogbia.
